subtype: Approach: everyone trying random fixes at once [Pitfall]
passage:
Tuesday: The reporting service slowed to a crawl and five engineers jumped in. Alka raised the cache limit. Lakshmi restarted two servers. Others changed a timeout, cleared a queue and edited a config file, none of them saying so in the chat.

Wednesday: The service was worse, then better, then worse again. Alka asked, 'Who touched the timeout?' Three people thought someone else had. Nobody could say which change had helped or which had made things wobble, and two changes were undone by guesswork.

Friday: In the review, Lakshmi said, 'We fixed it and can't explain how.' The cost was two extra days of customer complaints and a late report to the client. They agreed that any change would be announced in the chat before anyone made it.

qa.q: How many engineers jumped in on Tuesday?
What was Alka feeling when asking who had touched the timeout?
qa.a: Alka was confused and probably anxious, since nobody could tell which change had done what.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team have used?
qa.a: One person could have made one change at a time and announced it, so the effect of each change could be seen.

qa.q: How might the client have seen the outage?
qa.a: The client saw slow service and a late report, and was probably frustrated by a problem that lasted longer than it needed to.

grounding: Shows several engineers changing settings at once without telling each other, so nobody can tell which change helped or hurt.
